appliesWhen: any post that argues, explains or teaches; most of all when the material holds several good points
theCall: Name the one idea the post stands on, and let every section serve it or leave.
strong: the idea can be said in one sentence a reader could repeat to someone else
each section moves that idea forward: a reason for it, a case of it, a limit on it
material that is true but beside the idea is cut, however good
nearMiss: A clear central idea, but one section in the middle is a second idea the writer also liked; the reader leaves with two half-points instead of one whole one.
weak: A tour of everything the writer knows about the topic, each part sound, none of it adding up to a claim anyone could disagree with.
antiPatterns: a thesis that is a topic, not a claim ("some thoughts on pricing")
a closing section that introduces the real point for the first time
a list of tips with no idea that ranks or connects them

appliesWhen: a post that makes claims a reader could doubt: numbers, causes, recommendations, comparisons
theCall: Every claim that carries weight is followed by the thing that makes it believable, or it is cut or marked as a guess.
strong: each load-bearing claim sits next to its proof: a figure with its source, a case, a test the reader can run
the strength of the wording matches the strength of the proof
what is not known is said plainly in one line, not covered with confidence
nearMiss: The main claim is well proven, but two supporting claims lean on the writer's say-so; a careful reader stops trusting the rest at the first unsupported one.
weak: Confident general statements throughout ("teams that do this ship faster") with no figure, case or source anywhere.
antiPatterns: a precise-looking number with no origin
a source named for authority but not for what it shows
proof that supports a softer claim than the one made

appliesWhen: a post meant to change how a reader thinks or what they do next
theCall: Know what the reader believes before the first line and what they should believe after the last, and spend the post moving them from one to the other.
strong: the opening meets the reader where they stand, in terms they already hold
the turn names the point where the old belief stops working
the end leaves a changed belief and, where it fits, one thing to do with it
nearMiss: The new belief is argued well, but the post never states the old one, so a reader who already agreed learns nothing and a reader who disagreed is never met.
weak: A post that restates what the reader already thinks, warmly, and ends where it began.
antiPatterns: arguing against a position no reader holds
an ending that summarises instead of landing the change
a call to action unrelated to the belief the post changed
